messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At seventy-eight, Omar had spent over fifty years as a roofer, his hands shaped by the trade and his face weathered by the sun. He was a man who found comfort in structure and routine, but for the last six months, his world had felt dangerously unstable. The trouble began on a hot August morning while resealing the roof of a local elementary school. He was working with Karim, the son of his oldest friend, when a drum of industrial solvent ruptured. The fumes were overwhelming, a toxic cloud that sent them scrambling. Omar made it to the edge, but Karim was overcome, collapsing on the hot tar paper. Omar remembers the sounds most vividly: the panicked shouts from the playground below as teachers rushed children inside, the approaching sirens, and his own ragged, burning breaths as he tried to drag Karim to safety.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that day behaved strangely. When the insurance adjusters or company lawyers asked him to recount the sequence of events, Omar found the details slippery, the timeline dissolving into a fog of panic. He struggled to deliberately access the memory he needed to provide a clear statement. Yet, at other times, the memory would force its way into his mind when he least wanted it to. Sometimes it was an image of Karim’s face, slack and pale; other times, it was just a feeling, a wave of pure, chemical terror that would wash over him without any clear image attached, leaving him breathless and disoriented.

These intrusions soon became linked to the world around him. The sight of his own grandchildren playing in the yard was enough to bring on a fragment of the memory, the sound of their laughter twisting into the panicked shouts from the school playground. This connection solidified quickly; seeing children, once a source of simple joy, now served as a direct portal back to the worst moment of his life. A news report on an industrial fire or seeing Karim’s father at the market would have the same effect, each trigger plunging him back into the sensory chaos of the accident.

The constant threat of these memories has left Omar in a state of perpetual, exhausting vigilance. He is unable to relax, even in the familiar comfort of his own home. He describes a wire pulled taut inside his chest, vibrating with an alarm that never ceases. His wife, Layla, has learned not to touch him without announcing herself first, as an unexpected hand on his shoulder can make him flinch so violently he once knocked a cup of coffee from her hand. Sleep offers little escape, with hours spent staring at the ceiling, his mind replaying the day’s near-misses with potential triggers. This constant state of high alert makes him scan his environment relentlessly, which in turn makes him even more likely to spot the very things that torment him. The low hum of a television in the other room becomes a potential source of a triggering news report; a trip to the grocery store becomes a tense exercise in avoiding Karim’s family.

The terror carried by the memories is so absolute that it has reinforced his fear of the triggers themselves. He has come to believe that the memories are not just painful, but dangerous, capable of overwhelming him completely. As a result, he has begun to see the potential for disaster everywhere, especially around the children he so loves. He no longer visits his son’s family, making excuses that his old bones ache too much for the drive. The joy he once took in his grandchildren has been replaced by a gnawing fear that their presence will unleash something inside him he cannot control. It was Layla who finally insisted he seek help, after finding him sitting alone in the dark for the third night in a row. Omar came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, admitting that his greatest fear was no longer what happened on that roof, but that he would spend the rest of his years a prisoner in his own home, a stranger to his own family.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory leads to an increased awareness of or scanning for triggers.
